messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lukas had been on a hiking trip with two friends in the mountains when the weather changed with shocking speed. What began as a clear afternoon on a wooded trail became sheets of rain, wind that snapped branches overhead, and then a landslide that tore across the path below them, cutting off the route back to the car. He remembered the sound first more than the sight: a deep, grinding roar, then the sharp crack of trees giving way. For a stretch of time afterward, there were parts he could not account for at all, and even now he could not force those gaps to fill in. When he tried to describe the worst moments, he said it was like being flooded by the feeling of terror without a full picture attached, as if his body still knew what happened before his mind could arrange it into a story.

In the weeks after, Lukas found that anything that placed him back in a similar kind of exposed space could bring the experience rushing up at him. A tree-lined park near his apartment, a trail he used to enjoy on weekends, even open stretches of ground on the edge of the city could suddenly make him feel as if he were back on that mountainside. At work as a salesperson, he started avoiding client meetings that involved outdoor venues or showrooms with panoramic glass views onto green space, telling himself the setting did not matter while privately feeling his chest tighten the moment he stepped into them. He had come to believe that nature itself had turned dangerous, but more than that, that his own sense of being emotionally vulnerable was dangerous too: if he let himself relax, he would be caught off guard again. Those moments left him questioning who he was now, because the version of himself who used to be easygoing and confident on the road no longer felt recognizable to him. He also began to feel that nothing in his life had much meaning if it could be swept away so quickly, and the sense that he could not rely on other people deepened when he remembered how powerless he and his friends had been, waiting for help that felt far too slow to come.

That same belief that others could not be depended on shaped the way he responded at night. Lukas woke repeatedly to check whether he was safe, listening for sounds outside his apartment and scanning the room before he could settle again, as if danger might be waiting just beyond the door. During the day he stayed superalert, watching exits, sizing up ground under his feet, and tracking weather forecasts with an intensity that exhausted him. He noticed that when he was already feeling exposed or uncertain, a brief memory fragment could hit with full force: a flash of the trail, the roar of the slide, the helplessness in his own body, and with it the same terror he had felt in the mountains. Sometimes, without any clear image at all, he was simply overtaken by the emotion itself, and once that happened he would think he had to stay on guard because the world had already shown him it could become catastrophic without warning. In that state, his mind went back to the event again and again, not gently but as a fresh assault, and each return seemed to make the fear more immediate.

The more Lukas lived with that sense of danger, the more he began to treat ordinary places as potential threats. A walk through a park on the way to a client meeting could be enough to set off the feeling that something was about to happen, especially if he noticed himself feeling emotionally open or tired. The old memory would surface, terror would surge, and then he would decide he had been right not to trust the setting, not to trust his own calm, and not to trust other people to keep him safe. That sequence narrowed his world. He stopped taking appointments that required travel to rural areas, declined invitations to hike with friends, and became increasingly tense even in city spaces that reminded him of being outdoors. The change was visible to people around him, but Lukas said the larger injury was internal: he did not know himself anymore, and the future felt stripped of meaning.

By the time he sought help, Lukas was tired of living as if he were still stranded on that mountain, checking the night, bracing for images or feelings he could not control, and avoiding anything that hinted at vulnerability or open space. He came in saying he wanted to feel normal again, but what frightened him most was the possibility that he would never again feel like himself, or ever be able to trust that life could hold meaning without always waiting for the next disaster.
